subject: English
passage: Nineteenth-century philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche is renowned for his declaration that "God is dead," which he supposedly used to articulate a comprehensive critique of Western religious and moral foundations. Note "supposedly": as scholar Walter Kaufmann has demonstrated, Nietzsche employs this phrase only twice in his extensive writings—to make a specific point about the cultural shift toward secularization—and it remained relatively obscure until some mid-twentieth-century existentialist philosophers seeking to establish intellectual authority for their atheistic worldview transformed it into a central philosophical doctrine.
prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Although Nietzsche is renowned for his declaration that "God is dead," the phrase was relatively obscure until philosophers in the mid-twentieth century came to recognize that the declaration was a comprehensive critique that anticipated their own views.
choices.B: Some mid-twentieth-century existentialist philosophers gave Nietzsche's declaration that "God is dead" a significance it does not have in Nietzsche's work, but it is nevertheless an effective critique of Western religious and moral foundations.
choices.C: The fame of Nietzsche's declaration that "God is dead" is not due to the importance of the phrase in Nietzsche's work but rather to the promotion of the phrase by some later philosophers for their own purposes.
choices.D: Nietzsche's declaration that "God is dead" has been interpreted as a comprehensive critique of religious foundations, but it was intended as a focused observation about cultural secularization.

explanation:
Choice C is the best answer because it most accurately states the main idea of the text. The text explains that philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche's famous declaration that "God is dead" was supposedly (that is, widely assumed but not proven) intended to articulate a comprehensive critique of Western religious and moral foundations. The text then emphasizes the lack of supporting evidence for this idea by calling out the term "supposedly," and explaining that, according to Walter Kaufmann, Nietzsche used the phrase only twice in his works, in reference to specific circumstances related to cultural secularization, and that the phrase didn't gain prominence until existentialist philosophers in the mid-twentieth century elevated it to a central doctrine and thereby implied that Nietzsche shared some of their atheistic views. By emphasizing "supposedly," the text implies that there is no independent reason to believe that Nietzsche would agree with the phrase's use outside of the specific context for which he wrote it and that, therefore, the mid-twentieth-century philosophers who used it did so to support their own views without regard for the phrase's importance to Nietzsche's work.

Why B is incorrect:

Choice B is incorrect. Although the text indicates that some mid-twentieth-century existentialist philosophers altered the significance of Nietzsche's declaration, the text doesn't suggest that the phrase is an "effective critique" of Western religious and moral foundations, let alone that this effectiveness is unaffected by taking the phrase out of its original context.
